description: F-CORE-041: `personalDataDescription` reports WHERE operator-supplied text can come to rest in these books, and how much of it is actually there. It is the counterpart to `systemDescription`, which answers the same shape of question about auditing — and it exists because the alternative was a hand-written inventory, which is the kind of list that goes stale in silence: a renamed field leaves the row standing, still readable, still wrong. THE SPLIT IS THE POINT AND IT FALLS ON SUMMAE'S OWN AXIS. Where identifying data can sit is mechanism: the partner has a name, the trail records an actor, a posting carries free text, and that is as true in the us pack as in the de pack. Whether a given field COUNTS as personal data is not mechanism — jurisdictions answer it differently, and a company identifier is personal data for a sole trader and not for a corporation. So the projection never classifies; it says `freeText` (summae neither constrains nor interprets this content) and it counts. `classification` states that in the payload, so a reader cannot mistake an inventory for legal advice. IT REPORTS SHAPE, NEVER CONTENT: `present` is how many partners carry an address, not what any address says; `addressKeys` is which keys occur, not their values. A projection built to help with a privacy obligation must not become the convenient place to read everybody's data out of. `addressKeys` is also the answer a hand-written list cannot give: the format declares a recommended address shape and does not forbid others, so the only truthful answer to what is in there is to look. Two of the rows carry `present: null` on purpose — a posting text and an audit diff exist per record rather than per holder, and inventing a count for them would be a number nobody could act on. | Successor to `personal-data-description`, and what moved is the one thing that was never this fixture's subject: the expectation pinned the COMPLETE `fields` list, so summae could not admit to holding operator text in a sixth place without the suite going red. That is the same weld `system-description-claims` was created for one folder over, and the argument is unchanged — the completeness IS the contract, the length of the list is the product's. It went red for the reason predicted: three fields that were missing all along (asset.name, provision.reason, deferral.reason — IMPL-045) were added, and each of them is a place where a name really can end up. What this fixture pins is everything else: the counts, the address keys a tenant actually holds, and the sentence that says summae classifies nothing. The list itself is now guarded better than a literal can guard it — `GdprConformanceDocTest` / `gdpr-conformance-doc.test.ts` hold the projection's rows against the § 1 inventory of docs/gdpr-conformance.md AND against format.schema.json, in both directions and both languages, so neither a field that stops existing nor one that is quietly added survives.

expect.comment: No address and no VAT id — the counts must distinguish the two partners, or `present` would just be the partner count under another name.

Two partners, one with an address and a VAT id; one voucher with an issuer; two distinct actors across the trail. The address keys are the four that were actually used, sorted — deterministic ordering, like every other list summae publishes. | The `fields` list is deliberately not pinned here — see the description: it is a census the product grows, guarded by the two conformance-doc tests instead.
expect.classification: none — summae reports where operator-supplied text can sit, not which of it is personal data under any jurisdiction
